extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interpreting and construing patent claim language during examination, including when to apply ordinary meaning, special definitions, the broadest reasonable interpretation, the effect of preambles and transitional phrases, contingent clauses, and printed-matter analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of a claim term that does not invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow flowchart: first determine whether a claim term has an ordinary and customary meaning to those of ordinary skill in the art. If so, check the specification for a special definition; if none, apply the ordinary and customary meaning. If the specification provides a special definition, use it. If a claim term does not have an ordinary and customary meaning, check the specification for a meaning; if no reasonably clear meaning can be ascribed after considering the specification and prior art, apply the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and object to the specification under 37 CFR 1.75(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a presumption that claim terms have their ordinary and customary meaning and the specification must provide a clear and intentional use of a special definition for the claim term to be treated as having a special definition. When a special definition exists, an Office action should acknowledge and identify it. If no clear meaning exists after reviewing specification and prior art, apply BRI and take appropriate procedural steps (e.g., 112(b) rejection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit disavowal / narrowing in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If the broadest reasonable interpretation of a claim is narrower than the words otherwise suggest as the result of implicit disavowal in the specification, the examiner should make the interpretation clear on the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the claim wording appears broad, consistent and exclusive depiction or statements in the specification may implicitly disavow broader meanings; the examiner should articulate such narrowed interpretation in the file history (record). See also reference to MPEP § 2173.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of the preamble (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The determination of whether a preamble limits a claim is made on a case-by-case basis in light of the facts in each case; a claim preamble has the import that the claim as a whole suggests for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use caselaw guideposts (e.g., Catalina, Bell Comm., Pitney Bowes) and read the preamble in context of the entire claim to decide whether it is limiting. There is no single litmus test; evaluate whether the preamble gives 'life, meaning, and vitality' to the claim or merely states purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble statements limiting structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Any terminology in the preamble that limits the structure of the claimed invention must be treated as a claim limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve by reviewing the entirety of the application to understand what the inventors actually invented and intended to encompass, without importing extraneous specification limitations. If preamble language supplies structural elements missing from the body, treat it as limiting (cases: Corning, Pac‑Tec, In re Stencel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble statements reciting purpose or intended use
rubrics_metrics.description: Preamble recitations that merely state the purpose or intended use of the invention are generally not considered claim limitations when the body of the claim fully and intrinsically sets forth all the limitations of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the preamble's stated purpose results in a structural (or, for process claims, manipulative) difference from the prior art. If the preamble was relied on during prosecution to distinguish prior art (clear reliance), the preamble may become limiting. Use cases (Shoes by Firebug, Pitney Bowes, Jansen, Metabolite) as guidance and check prosecution history for reliance on preamble to define invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase: 'comprising' (open-ended)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitional term 'comprising' (synonymous with 'including,' 'containing,' or 'characterized by') is inclusive or open-ended and does not exclude additional, unrecited elements or method steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims using 'comprising' as allowing additional elements or steps beyond those recited (see Mars, Invitrogen, Genentech, Moleculon, Gillette). When combined with closed Markush groupings, interpret that the Markush members are closed but the overall claim may still permit additional components due to 'comprising.' See MPEP § 2117 for Markush discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase: 'consisting of' (closed)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitional phrase 'consisting of' excludes any element, step, or ingredient not specified in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'consisting of' as closing the claim to unrecited elements (subject to context-specific factual exceptions where unrelated items do not affect the invention). When 'consisting of' appears in a clause of the claim body, there is an exceptionally strong presumption that the clause is closed. Consider Markush selection and whether dependent claims attempt to add elements to a 'consisting of' claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrase: 'consisting essentially of' (middle ground)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Consisting essentially of' limits the scope of a claim to the specified materials or steps 'and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)' of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground between 'consisting of' and 'comprising.' For prior art searching under 102/103, absent a clear specification indication of what the basic and novel characteristics are, treat 'consisting essentially of' as equivalent to 'comprising.' If applicant contends exclusion of additional components, the applicant bears the burden of showing material change to basic/novel characteristics. Examples and caselaw provided (In re Herz, PPG, AK Steel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other transitional phrases ('having', 'composed of', etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional phrases such as 'having' must be interpreted in light of the specification to determine whether open or closed claim language is intended; 'composed of' may be interpreted as 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' depending on facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume uniform meaning; determine intended scope from intrinsic evidence. Case law (Lampi, Crystal Semiconductor, Regents v. Eli Lilly, AFG, In re Bertsch) shows context-driven interpretation; e.g., 'having' sometimes construed open, sometimes not presumptively open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clauses 'adapted to', 'adapted for', 'wherein', 'whereby' (may be limiting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim scope is not necessarily limited by language that suggests or makes optional but does not require steps to be performed; however, 'adapted to/adapted for' clauses and 'wherein/whereby' clauses may raise a question as to limiting effect and the determination depends on the specific facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the clause provides meaning and purpose to manipulative steps or the written description shows a narrower meaning (e.g., designed for a specific use), treat the clause as limiting. Where a 'whereby' clause states a condition material to patentability, it cannot be ignored. But a 'whereby' clause that only expresses intended result of a positively recited step may be given no weight (see Griffin, Giannelli, Hoffer, Minton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingent limitations (method vs system claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: For method claims, the broadest reasonable interpretation of contingent limitations requires only steps that must be performed (steps conditional on events are not required unless the condition must occur). For system claims, if the claimed structure performs a function only when a condition precedent is met, the system claim still requires structure for performing the function should the condition occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether the claimed invention can be practiced without the condition; if so, contingent steps are not required for method claims. For system claims, the structure must be present even if the function is not executed. See Ex parte Schulhauser for detailed analysis and PTAB reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter / functional vs nonfunctional descriptive material
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation is 'printed matter' only if it claims the content of information. Once determined to be printed matter, the next inquiry is whether the printed matter is functionally or structurally related to the associated physical substrate; only if ‘yes’ should the printed matter be given patentable weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First determine whether the limitation claims content of information (In re DiStefano). If printed matter, assess whether a new and nonobvious functional relationship to the substrate exists (In re Lowry, In re Ngai, In re Gulack). Evidence of functional relationship includes instances where the printed matter performs a function with respect to the product (e.g., indicia on a measuring cup) or where the product's physical structure enables an algorithm/information to be satisfied. If no functional relationship, the printed matter is given no patentable weight. Apply analogous inquiry for method claims where instructional limitations are added to known methods (applicant must show new functional relationship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence supporting or opposing functional relationship for printed matter
rubrics_metrics.description: To give printed matter patentable weight, show evidence that the printed matter and product are in a functional relationship (e.g., printed indicia performs a function; the product performs a function with respect to the printed matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive evidence: indicia that perform functions (measuring marks), product structure that arranges information to satisfy claimed algorithm. Negative evidence: absence of any functional interaction between information content and physical substrate. Use relevant case law (Lowry, Gulack, Miller) to evaluate the nature of the relationship.
